chapter.title: Tutorial
chapter.para: This chapter is a hands-on introduction to Scaly. It gets you from an empty file to a running program, then takes you on a quick tour of the language. Later chapters cover everything here in depth; the goal now is to write and run real code as fast as possible.

section.title: Getting Started
section.para: To try Scaly before installing anything, a browser is enough. The tour at scaly.io/play/tour.html runs the programs of step by step, and you can change them; the REPL at scaly.io/play is the interactive session of . The compiler runs in the browser tab itself: nothing is sent anywhere.

section.title: Installing Scaly
section.para: Scaly is installed by one command. On macOS and Linux, in a terminal:
section.programlisting: curl -fsSL https://scaly.io/install.sh | sh
section.para: On macOS 26.4 and newer, Terminal stops a pasted command that downloads something with a warning, Possible Malware, Paste Blocked — this one too. Choose Paste Anyway; the script it runs can be read first at scaly.io/install.sh.
On Windows, in PowerShell ( says what happens there, and how to work with Visual Studio):
section.programlisting: irm https://scaly.io/install.ps1 | iex
section.para: Open a new terminal afterwards. The installer has put three commands on your PATH: scaly, the tool you will use most, scalyc, the compiler by itself, and scalyls, the language server your editor talks to. Everything else it installed lives in ~/.scaly. has the details: which systems get Scaly ready to run, what the others need, how to ask for a particular version, and how to remove it again.

section.title: Hello, World!
section.para: A Scaly program is just a file of statements — there is no main function to declare and nothing to import. Put this single line in a file called hello.scaly:
section.programlisting: print("Hello, World!")
section.para: Run it:
section.programlisting: scaly run hello.scaly
section.para: The program prints:
scaly run compiles the file in memory and runs it at once; nothing is left on disk. To get a program you can keep and hand to someone else, build it:
section.programlisting: scaly build hello.scaly -o hello ./hello
section.para: Add --release for the optimised build: the whole program — your code, the standard library and every package it uses — is optimised as one piece.

scaly new hello writes such a start for you: a directory hello with hello.scaly in it — a function, a test for it (scaly test hello.scaly runs every function whose name begins with test) and the line that prints.
That is the whole edit-compile-run loop. Everything that follows is just more interesting things to put between the braces.

section.title: Trying Things Out
section.para: scaly without arguments starts an interactive session. An expression shows its value and its type; a let or var keeps a value for the entries that follow:
section.screen: $ scaly scaly> 6 * 7 it: int = 42 scaly> let name "Scaly" name: String = "Scaly" scaly> :where name name: String the value 8 bytes, on the session page of its entry its text 5 bytes, on a page of its own scaly> :quit
section.para: :where shows where a value lives — Scaly manages memory in regions, and here you can watch it do so. :help lists the other commands.

section.title: Using Scaly with VS Code
section.para: You can drive the whole edit-compile-run-debug loop from Visual Studio Code. The Scaly extension provides syntax highlighting and connects the editor to the scalyls language server you installed in — giving live error squiggles, hover, go-to-definition, completion, rename, and more.
If you do not have VS Code yet, download it from code.visualstudio.com (installers for macOS, Windows and Linux; on Ubuntu, sudo snap install code --classic also works).

section.title: Installing the Scaly Extension
section.para: The Scaly extension is distributed as a .vsix package on scaly.io. Download scaly.io/downloads/scaly-vscode.vsix, then install it from within VS Code: open the Extensions view, click the ··· menu in its title bar, choose Install from VSIX…, and pick the downloaded file.

The extension launches scalyls from your PATH, so install the toolchain first (). If VS Code was already running when you installed the toolchain, restart it (not just the window) so its process picks up the updated PATH. Should the server binary live somewhere unusual, point the scaly.server.path setting at it.

section.title: What the Language Server Gives You
section.para: Open any folder, create a file double.scaly, and type a small program:
section.programlisting:
function double(n: int) returns int n * 2
let d double(21) if d = 42 print("doubled!")
section.para: As you type, the language server is at work. Things to try:

listitem.para: Diagnostics — misspell a call (say, change double(21) to doubel(21)): a red squiggle appears and the Problems panel shows function not found: doubel. Fix it and the squiggle clears.
Hover — rest the mouse on double or a binding to see its signature or type.
Go to Definition (F12) and Find All References (Shift+F12) — work across files and into the standard library.
Completion — names in scope and members appear as you type.
Rename (F2) — renames a symbol everywhere it is used, shadow-aware.
Outline and symbols — the Outline view and Cmd+Shift+O list the file's functions and types; Cmd+T searches symbols across the workspace. (Use Ctrl instead of Cmd on Linux.)
Inlay hints — inferred types appear inline after bindings; signature help shows parameter hints while you type a call; semantic highlighting and folding come for free.

section.para: If the server ever needs a kick — say, after you rebuilt it — run Scaly: Restart Language Server from the Command Palette.

section.title: Run, Build and Test
section.para: The extension offers three tasks for the file in the active editor, with no tasks.json to write. Terminal > Run Task… lists them under scaly:

listitem.para: scaly run: the program is compiled in memory and runs in the terminal panel.
scaly build -g: the program, with debug information, beside the file. ⇧⌘B (Ctrl+Shift+B) offers it.

section.para: A compiler error lands in the Problems panel, a click away from its line. To change a task — another output, an argument —, choose Terminal > Configure Tasks… and pick it: VS Code writes it into .vscode/tasks.json, where it can be edited.

section.title: Starting the Debugger
section.para: Debugging needs nothing more. The extension drives lldb-dap, the debugger that comes with Apple's Command Line Tools (the installer fetches them where they are missing), with Xcode, and with LLVM — on Ubuntu, sudo apt install lldb-21. Open a .scaly file and press F5: the extension builds it with debug information and starts it under the debugger. Should lldb-dap live somewhere unusual, point the scaly.debugAdapter.path setting at it.

On Windows the extension debugs with the Visual Studio debugger instead, the one Windows programs are debugged with: a build with debug information writes a .pdb beside the program, as the Visual Studio Build Tools do for C++ (the installer fetched them for scaly build). VS Code has that debugger through Microsoft's C/C++ extension; the first F5 offers to install it, and everything after that works as described here — the same F5, the same launch.json, strings and containers shown by their contents ().

For a configuration of your own — arguments, an environment, another program — you write a .vscode/launch.json, and that needs a folder open (File > Open Folder…), not just a file. Open the Run and Debug view: the icon with the play triangle and the bug in the Activity Bar on the left, or ⇧⌘D (Ctrl+Shift+D). As long as the folder has no launch.json, the view shows a Run and Debug button — the same as F5 — and beneath it the link create a launch.json file. Click the link with a .scaly file in the editor; should VS Code ask which debugger, choose Scaly. It writes the file, opens it, and what it writes debugs the open file:
source is built before the launch; program names an executable to debug as it is, and args, env and cwd go to the program.

A launch.json may hold several configurations; the drop-down at the top of the Run and Debug view chooses the one F5 starts. Here the first builds greet.scaly and runs it with two arguments, a variable in its environment and the workspace folder as its working directory; the second debugs a program that is already built — with scaly build -g, or there are no line tables for a breakpoint to bind to:

section.title: Breakpoints in Scaly Files
section.para: VS Code only lets you set breakpoints in files whose language an installed extension has declared debuggable. The Scaly extension from does exactly that for .scaly files, so with it installed, clicking in the editor gutter places a breakpoint (a red dot appears) — nothing to configure.

section.title: Setting a Breakpoint and Stepping
section.para: Put this program in area.scaly in your workspace folder. It computes a rectangle's area from two mutable bindings — small, but enough to stop and inspect some values:
section.programlisting: var width 8 var height 5 var area width * height if area = 40 print("the area is 40") else print("unexpected area")
section.para: Click in the gutter to the left of the var area width * height line to set a breakpoint (a red dot appears), then press F5. The program builds and runs, and execution stops at that line before it executes — at which point width and height already have values but area does not yet.
With execution paused you can:

listitem.para: Read width and height in the Variables pane, or hover them in the editor to see their values.
Step one line at a time with F10 (Step Over) — after stepping past the breakpoint line, area appears with the value 40. Step into a called function with F11.
Press F5 again to continue to the program's end.

section.para: Breakpoints, stepping, and variable inspection all rely on the -g debug information; without it the program still runs, but the debugger has no source lines to stop on.

section.title: Stepping into Functions and the Call Stack
section.para: Stepping becomes more interesting once a function is involved. F10 (Step Over) runs a call as a single step; F11 (Step Into) descends into the called function so you can watch it run. Put this program in rectangle.scaly in your workspace folder — it factors the area calculation out into a function:
section.programlisting:
function area(w: int, h: int) returns int { var result w * h result }
var width 8 var height 5 var a area(width, height) if a = 40 print("the area is 40") else print("unexpected area")
section.para: Set a breakpoint on the var a area(width, height) line and press F5. When execution stops there, width and height show in the Variables pane. Now press F11 instead of F10: the editor jumps into the body of area and stops on var result w * h.

The Call Stack pane (bottom-left of the Run and Debug view) now lists two frames — area on top and main below it — showing exactly how you got here. Click a frame to switch the Variables pane and the editor to that frame's context: selecting main shows width and height again, while area shows its own local result (still unassigned at this point, just as area was before its line ran in the previous example).
From inside the function you can keep stepping, press Shift+F11 (Step Out) to return to the caller, or F5 to continue to the end. The function-and-procedure model is covered in and .

section.title: What the Debugger Shows
section.para: For whichever stack frame is selected:

listitem.para: Breakpoints land on top-level statements, bindings and function bodies, and line by line inside loop and conditional bodies — on a single statement within a while, for, if or choose, not just on the statement around it.

The Variables pane shows a function's arguments and its let and var bindings: numbers and booleans; structures, unions and pointers with their fields to expand, a union's variant by its name; a String as its text; a Vector, Array or List with its elements.
The Watch view and Debug Console evaluate expressions as C/C++ and do not understand Scaly names. To read a value, use the Variables pane or hover over the name in the editor.

section.title: Scaly on Windows
section.para: Everything in this chapter works on Windows 10 and 11, on x64 and on arm64. This section collects what is different there: how the installation goes, what a program looks like on disk, and how to debug one — in VS Code, and in Visual Studio itself.

section.title: Installing on Windows
section.para: Open PowerShell (or Windows Terminal) and run:
section.programlisting: irm https://scaly.io/install.ps1 | iex
section.para: No administrator rights are needed for Scaly itself: it goes to %USERPROFILE%\.scaly, and its three programs are put on your own PATH.

Building a program needs one thing Windows does not bring along: a linker, and the C runtime's libraries to link with. Scaly uses the ones of the Visual Studio Build Tools (the C++ tools and a Windows SDK), as Rust does on Windows. The installer looks for them, and where they are missing it fetches them through winget. Windows then asks once for administrator rights, and the download is several gigabytes, so this step takes a few minutes. If Visual Studio with the workload Desktop development with C++ is installed already, the installer finds it and fetches nothing.
To decide for yourself, set SCALY_BUILD_TOOLS before running the installer — ask asks first, skip leaves them out:
section.programlisting: $env:SCALY_BUILD_TOOLS = "ask" irm https://scaly.io/install.ps1 | iex
section.para: Without the Build Tools, scaly run, scaly test and the REPL work all the same; only scaly build says that it has nothing to link with, and how to install it. Open a new terminal when the installer is done, so that it sees the new PATH.

section.title: Programs and Debug Information
section.para: The commands are the ones of ; a program you build is an .exe:
section.programlisting: scaly run hello.scaly scaly build hello.scaly -o hello.exe .\hello.exe
section.para: With -g the build writes a second file beside the program, hello.pdb: the debug information, in the form every Windows debugger reads. It also carries the views that show a String as its text and a Vector, Array or List with its elements, so a debugger shows them without any setting — Visual Studio, VS Code and WinDbg alike:
section.programlisting: scaly build -g area.scaly -o area.exe

section.title: VS Code on Windows
section.para: Install VS Code from code.visualstudio.com or with winget install Microsoft.VisualStudioCode, then the Scaly extension as in . Start VS Code after Scaly is installed, so that it finds scalyls on the PATH.

Debugging uses the Visual Studio debugger, which VS Code gets from Microsoft's C/C++ extension. Open area.scaly from , set a breakpoint and press F5. The first time, the Scaly extension says that the C/C++ extension is missing and offers Install C/C++; install it and press F5 again. From then on everything in and applies as written; a launch.json takes the same attributes as on the other systems.

section.title: Visual Studio
section.para: Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 — the Community edition will do — debugs a Scaly program with the debugger it uses for C++. It needs the workload Desktop development with C++, which also brings everything scaly build links with. Start Visual Studio after Scaly is installed, so that its tasks find scaly on the PATH.
Visual Studio has no Scaly project type; it works on a folder. Choose File > Open > Folder… and pick the folder that holds area.scaly. The Solution Explorer shows its files.

Building. Right-click area.scaly in the Solution Explorer and choose Configure Tasks. Visual Studio opens .vs\tasks.vs.json; replace its content with a task that builds the file with debug information:
Now the context menu of every .scaly file in the folder has Build; it writes area.exe and area.pdb beside the source, and the compiler's messages appear in the Output window.

Debugging. Right-click area.exe in the Solution Explorer and choose Set as Startup Item. Open area.scaly, click in the margin left of var area width * height (or put the cursor there and press F9) and press F5: the program stops at that line. F10 steps over a line, F11 into a function, and the Locals window shows the bindings — area becomes 40 after the step. To stop at the first statement instead, start with F11 rather than F5.

Arguments, a working directory or an environment for the program go into a debug configuration: right-click area.exe, choose Add Debug Configuration and then Default. Visual Studio writes .vs\launch.vs.json, where the entry can be extended:

Remember to build again after changing the source: the debugger runs the .exe as it is. Visual Studio does not know Scaly as a language yet, so the editor shows a .scaly file as plain text, and the Watch window evaluates C++, not Scaly; for highlighting, completion and the rest of the language server, edit in VS Code.

section.title: A Tour of Scaly
section.para: This section sweeps quickly across the language using small, complete programs. If something is not fully explained here, do not worry — every feature is covered in detail in the rest of this specification, and each part of the tour points you to the relevant chapter. Each program prints what it computes; print writes a line:
section.programlisting: print "Hello from Scaly"
section.para: The same tour runs in the browser, step by step: scaly.io/play/tour.html. There every program of this section stands in an editor with a Run button — change it, run it again, try what happens when you break it; Reset brings the original back. Nothing to install: the compiler runs in the browser tab.

section.title: Values and Bindings
section.para: Bind a value to a name with let. There is no equals sign — the name is followed directly by its value. Use var for a binding you intend to change, and := to change it. A semicolon starts a comment, and backticks inside a string put a value into the text.
section.programlisting: let answer 42 ; immutable binding var count 0 ; mutable binding count := count + 1 ; assignment is := print "answer is `answer`, count is `count`"
section.para: The equals sign = is reserved for comparison, so it never gets confused with assignment. See for the full lexical rules.

section.title: Operators and Operations
section.para: Operators are ordinary identifiers, not keywords baked into the grammar. An operation is read from left to right; when operators are chained, they combine by the binding strength the standard library gives them — multiplication binds tighter than addition, comparison weaker than both:
section.programlisting: ; 3 + 4 * 5 is 3 + 20, which is 23 — not 35 let result 3 + 4 * 5 if result = 23 print("got 23") else print("unexpected")
section.para: Parentheses group explicitly, and an operator written where a value is expected acts as a prefix (-x, not done, a - -2). A call takes its arguments before the operators around it combine, and a call without parentheses takes exactly one argument: print "hi" is print("hi"), but an argument that is itself a call takes its parentheses, print(describe(x)). See for the complete model, tuples and functions as values included.

section.title: Control Flow
section.para: if chooses between branches. Single-statement branches need no braces; the condition needs no parentheses:
section.programlisting: let n 7 if n < 0 print "negative" else if n = 0 print "zero" else print "positive"
section.para: while repeats as long as its condition holds. Use braces for a multi-statement body:
section.programlisting: var sum 0 var i 1 while i <= 10 { sum := sum + i i := i + 1 } print "the sum is `sum`"
section.para: for iterates. for i in 4 runs i from 0 up to — but not including — 4:
section.programlisting: var total 0 for i in 4 total := total + i print "0 + 1 + 2 + 3 is `total`"

section.title: Functions
section.para: A function declares its parameter types and return type. The value of the last expression is returned automatically — no return keyword is needed for the final result. A single-expression body needs no braces:
section.programlisting:
function add(a: int, b: int) returns int a + b
print "3 + 4 is `add(3, 4)`"
section.para: Functions can call themselves. Here is the classic factorial:
section.programlisting:
function factorial(n: int) returns int if n <= 1 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)
print "5! is `factorial(5)`"
section.para: Functions are pure: they read their arguments and return a value, with no side effects. To mutate, use a procedure.

section.title: Procedures and Mutation
section.para: A procedure is like a function but may change its inputs and perform side effects. It says which inputs it changes: a parameter it writes is marked mutable, the receiver this included, and a field that may change after the object is built is declared var. A reader always knows which calls can mutate state, and the compiler checks it. See for the details.

section.title: Structures and Methods
section.para: Define a structure by listing its fields. A structure with public fields gets a constructor that takes them in order. Methods are functions or procedures whose first parameter is this:
covers constructors, including explicit init forms with their own signatures.

section.title: Unions, Options, and choose
section.para: A union holds one of several variants. Each variant may carry a payload. The most common union is Option, which represents a value that may be absent:
Match on a union with choose. Each when clause names a binding, then the variant, then the result; the binding is bound to the variant's payload. An else clause handles the remaining variants:
section.programlisting:
define Option union(Some: int, None)
function or_zero(o: Option) returns int choose o when v: Some v else 0
print "`or_zero(Option.Some(7))` and `or_zero(Option.None)`"
section.para: See for union layout, the T? shorthand, and pattern matching in full.

section.title: Modules and Imports
section.para: Split a program across files with module: the statement module shapes loads the sibling file shapes.scaly. A type defined there stays hidden until the using file imports it with use:
Forgetting the import is caught at compile time, and the error states the exact use line to add. The standard library needs no imports — it is always visible.
Code that several programs share is a package, and a package somebody else wrote is one line away:
section.programlisting: package json 0.1.3 "github.com/someone/json"
section.para: scaly fetches it from that git repository the first time the program is run, tested or built; and scaly install builds the programs such a package offers and puts them on your PATH. See for packages and their sources, visibility rules, and glob imports.

section.title: Putting It Together
section.para: Let us combine the pieces into one small, complete program: a safe division that returns an Option instead of crashing on a zero divisor, with the caller deciding what to print.
Start with the function. It returns None when the divisor is zero, and Some with the quotient otherwise:
section.programlisting:
define Option union(Some: int, None)
function safe_divide(a: int, b: int) returns Option if b = 0 Option.None else Option.Some(a / b)
section.para: Now call it and react to the result with choose. The Some arm receives the quotient; the else arm handles division by zero:
section.programlisting: let result safe_divide(20, 4) choose result when q: Some if q = 5 print("20 / 4 = 5") else print("unexpected quotient") else print("cannot divide by zero")
section.para: Put both pieces in divide.scaly, then build and run it:
section.programlisting: scaly build divide.scaly -o divide ./divide
section.para: It prints:
Change the call to safe_divide(7, 0) and the same program prints cannot divide by zero — the union makes the failure a value you must handle, not a crash you can forget.
From here, the rest of this specification fills in the details: the rules, the full model, and the system including generics and the inferred region-based memory management.
